title: Module Onboarding Checklists are written after the first onboarding, and their absence never blocks a new module type
content:
A.1.10.2.5.1.1.1.3 defines Module Onboarding Checklists as use-case specific steps required when a Core Spell onboards a new module, then states how they come into existence: "Module Onboarding Checklists are **created after the first onboarding of a given module type, based on the learnings from that onboarding**. The absence of a Module Onboarding Checklist does not block the onboarding of a new module type."

Both halves matter. The first says a checklist is a distillation of what actually went wrong and right, not a speculative list written by someone imagining the work. Checklists written in advance tend to encode the author's expectations; ones written afterwards encode the surprises, which is where the value is.

The second prevents a common institutional failure. Once a process artifact is required, its absence becomes a blocker, and organizations end up unable to do anything genuinely new because the paperwork for novelty does not exist yet. Saying explicitly that a missing checklist is not a blocker preserves the ability to act first and codify second.

This is a different treatment of novelty from A.1.10.2.3.3, where an item with no precedent in the `spell-mainnet` archive is classified as novel and routed through a heavier process. The two are complementary: novel work gets *more scrutiny* (feasibility analysis, two-team agreement, possible audit) but not *procedural refusal*. Rigor scales up while permission stays available.

The result is a process library that grows monotonically from experience — the same logic as the Issue Retrospective at A.1.10.2.4.7.3.6, which asks what control was missing so that the answer can become a control.
description: A.1.10.2.5.1.1.1.3 makes checklists codified hindsight rather than a precondition, so process formation follows experience instead of gating it.
